question:
Let A be a stored real m-by-n matrix, with m at most n. Its wide thin-LQ routine transposes A, runs the full stored rectangular compiler on the transpose, extracts R as an m-by-m matrix from the residual, and extracts Q as an m-by-n matrix from the accumulated transform. Costs are vectors of nonnegative integer operation counters. Write C(X) for the actual counter vector of the rectangular compiler on stored input X, and P(N,M) for its declared polynomial upper budget, so C(X) is at most P(N,M) componentwise for every N-by-M X. For an N-by-M materialization whose entries each read one row and one entry, the exact counter vector is E(N,M)=2*N*M*tick(read)+(N*M+N)*(2*tick(read)+2*tick(write)). Here tick(op) is one unit in counter op and zero in the others. Let At be the actual stored transpose produced by the first stage.

Assess the assertion that the actual wide cost always equals E(n,m)+P(n,m)+E(m,m)+E(m,n). Give a concrete counterexample if it is false; the emit counter at m=n=1 is a useful discriminator. Then derive the exact additive identity in terms of C(At), and prove the resulting componentwise upper bound. Finally show that the R and Q returned by this same routine satisfy A=R*Q and Q*Q-transpose=I_m, including rank-deficient inputs and empty dimensions. Distinguish this wide routine from the all-shape dispatcher and keep operation counts separate from finite-bit runtime.
reference_answer:
The asserted equality with the polynomial budget is false. At m=n=1, take the stored zero matrix. The sole compiler column has no row below its pivot, so its column sweep emits no elimination record. Identity materialization and replay of the empty log emit nothing, as do the transpose and the two extractions. The actual wide emit counter is therefore zero. But P(1,1).emit=1 and all three E terms have emit counter zero. Thus the proposed budget equality would say 0=1. This witness concerns the actual fixed compiler, not a lower bound for optimal elimination.

Sequential Run.bind adds the costs of the actual executed stages. The transpose has exact cost E(n,m), and the extractions have exact costs E(m,m) and E(m,n), independent of their input values. Consequently cost(wide(A))=E(n,m)+C(At)+E(m,m)+E(m,n). The compiler's universal componentwise bound applies to this actual At, yielding cost(wide(A)) <= E(n,m)+P(n,m)+E(m,m)+E(m,n). Replacing the single actual compiler cost by an upper bound gives an inequality, not another exact identity. Materialization charges still apply to empty rows: E(N,0) includes the row surcharge. An empty compiler log still pays its end-marker read. None of these charges is an emit.

For correctness, let B be the residual and T the orthogonal transform returned by the compilation of At. Their denotations satisfy B=T*A-transpose, T-transpose*B=A-transpose and T-transpose*T=I_n. Transposing the recovery equation gives A=B-transpose*T. The residual satisfies B(k,i)=0 whenever i<k. Since every i is below m, all terms with k at least m vanish in each entry of B-transpose*T. Restricting that finite sum to the first m indices gives R(i,k)=B(k,i), Q(k,j)=T(k,j) and A=R*Q, exactly the two stored extractions. Because T is square and orthogonal, T*T-transpose=I_n as well; restricting its row indices to the first m rows gives Q*Q-transpose=I_m. No full-row-rank assumption was used: these are the deterministic stored factors even for zero or repeated rows. For m=0 the sums and I_m are empty, so the same statements hold; when n=0 the wide premise forces m=0. The library's wide_R/wide_Q and constructive wide_factorization/wide_orthogonal refinements establish precisely this same-run identity.

The all-shape compile dispatcher additionally charges one dimension comparison. That charge is not part of wide(A). These are counts in the extended exact-real stored-word model, including materialization and log operations, not finite-precision runtime, numerical stability or a gate-optimality theorem. This answer is a source-grounded mathematical reconstruction, not an admitted native Lean view or a new kernel certificate for all of the prose.
